title: Prospective randomized controlled clinical trial investigating ER:YAG laser therapy in patients with stress urinary incontinence
summary:
Urogynaecological conditions such as stress incontinence, vulvovaginal atrophy, the genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), and genital prolapse affect about half of all women at some point in their lives and significantly impair their quality of life. One such condition is stress incontinence, in which physical exertion, coughing, sneezing, or laughing leads to involuntary urine leakage. Causes are usually a weakness in the urethral sphincter mechanism, which is exacerbated by age, hormonal changes, pregnancies, childbirth, obesity, chronic cough, or connective tissue weakness. Changes in collagen metabolism and reduced collagen production play a particularly important role in this process.
Mild forms of stress incontinence are initially treated conservatively, for example with local estrogen therapy, pelvic floor exercises, physical therapy, or electrotherapy. In more severe or treatment-resistant cases, surgical procedures such as colposuspension or suburethral slings are used.
In recent years, laser therapy has also been investigated as a minimally invasive treatment option. 
CO₂ and ER:YAG lasers are primarily used for this purpose, as they create controlled thermal micro-injuries in the tissue. The ER:YAG laser, in particular, is considered gentle on tissue because it strongly absorbs water and thus heats less surrounding tissue. The goal of the treatment is to stimulate new collagen formation, improve microcirculation, and thicken the vaginal mucosa.
Animal studies and clinical trials have demonstrated positive histological changes, including improved collagen structure and tissue tightening. However, the scientific evidence regarding efficacy for stress incontinence remains inconsistent. Many studies report symptomatic improvements and good tolerability but exhibit methodological limitations such as small sample sizes, short follow-up periods, or the absence of placebo controls. Meta-analyses sometimes show only short-term effects. At the same time, studies confirm the overall good safety of the therapy, with predominantly mild and transient side effects. The current guideline therefore evaluates intravaginal laser therapy as a possible treatment option for mild to moderate stress incontinence.

interventions.name:
Arm 1 (Laser Therapy):
• 3 sessions of ER:YAG laser therapy: two-phase treatment using a 2940 nm erbium:YAG laser (Asclepion Laser Technologies, Jena, Germany) according to a standardized protocol at intervals of 4–6 weeks

Arm 2 (Control):
• 6 months of conservative therapy: local estrogen therapy, pelvic floor therapy (physical therapy, electrotherapy)
• Follow-up: 12 months after study enrollment

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Pre- and postmenopausal patients with stress urinary incontinence (SUI I–II)
2. Age ≥ 18 years
3. Written informed consent from the patient
4. Negative pregnancy test (urine β-hCG test)
5. Treatment-naive with regard to laser treatments for stress urinary incontinence
6. Patient is able to follow the study instructions and attend the required study visits (compliance)
7. Women of childbearing age: willing to use a reliable method of contraception during treatment
Exclusion criteria:
1. Concurrent participation in interventional studies or participation in an interventional study up to 30 days after the last intervention in that study
2. SUI Grade III, POP-Q ≥ 2, urge incontinence, overactive bladder, neurogenic bladder dysfunction
3. BMI > 35
4. Abnormal Pap smear, dysplasia of the vagina/vulva/cervix
5. Injuries/active infections in the area to be treated (vagina, introitus, vulva), previous surgeries in the area to be treated
6. Unexplained vaginal bleeding
7. Vaginal lesions and scars
8. Active or recent (within 30 days) infection of the urogenital tract (urinalysis) or hematuria
9. Malignancies of the anogenital region
10. Presence of an autoimmune disease
11. Use of photosensitive medications
12. Current or planned pregnancy or breastfeeding during the 6-month treatment phase, childbirth within the past year
13. Known or ongoing abuse of medications, drugs or alcohol
